faqs.a: The 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68 percent of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95 percent within 2, and 99.7 percent within 3. So with mean 100 and SD 15, expect roughly two-thirds of values between 85 and 115.

The Box-Muller transform converts two uniform random numbers into a standard normal value: z = sqrt(-2 ln u1) x cos(2 pi u2). Scaling by x = mean + SD x z gives any normal distribution. It is exact, not an approximation, and this tool uses it.
Because the bell curve is symmetric, the mean equals the median equals the mode. Extreme values are possible but rare: only about 0.3 percent fall beyond 3 standard deviations.
Set the standard deviation to 0.01 and every value lands within a hair of the mean. For truly constant output, just type the number directly; randomness is the wrong tool there.
faqs.q: How do I get nearly-constant values?

faqs.a: Use =NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) in Excel or Google Sheets, numpy.random.normal(mean, sd, n) in Python, or rnorm(n, mean, sd) in R. This tool is the no-install alternative for quick batches.

gaussian-random-number-generator.formula:

keyFacts: A normal (Gaussian) distribution is the bell curve: values cluster around the mean and taper symmetrically.
It is fully described by two numbers: the mean (center) and the standard deviation (spread).
The 68-95-99.7 rule: 68 percent within 1 SD, 95 percent within 2 SD, 99.7 percent within 3 SD.
Many real measurements are approximately normal: heights, weights, exam scores, measurement errors.
The Box-Muller transform turns uniform random numbers into exact normal values.

gaussian-random-number-generator.workedExample:
Simulating exam scores with mean 100 and SD 15:
1. Generate 1,000 values. Sample mean comes out near 100, sample SD near 15.
2. Check the 68 percent rule: count values between 85 and 115. Expect about 680 of 1,000.
3. Probability of scoring below 115: z = (115 - 100) / 15 = 1, so P = 84.1 percent.
4. Top 2.5 percent threshold: mean + 2 SD = 130. About 25 of 1,000 values exceed it.
The histogram shows the classic bell shape, tallest at 100.
